title: Comparing two symbolized models
text: compare_symbolic structural. tells ’s different specification two fits — submodels exist, predictors one, assumptions changed status. default return four slots: meta — class / family / response / n_obs side. diff_submodels — presence per submodel: left_only, right_only, . diff_terms — presence per (submodel, term_label) pair. diff_assumptions — left_status, right_status, same_status logical. pass metrics = TRUE fifth slot appears: diff_metrics — AIC, BIC, log-likelihood, df side plus delta column (right - left). Refuses compute deltas two fits obviously incomparable (different family, response, n_obs) instead carries comparable = FALSE attribute plus note explaining . fit-time identifiability convergence diagnostics — singular Hessian, parameter--boundary, near-zero variance components — compare_symbolic tool. Run drmTMB::check_drm() (gllvmTMB analogue) fit interpreting structural diff. compare surface assumes fits actually converged.

what: 2. Worked example 1: full versus reduced fixed effects
title: Comparing two symbolized models
text: common workflow fit richer model simpler nested model data ask whether richer model worth extra parameters. structural diff metrics: Model summaries Submodels Terms Assumptions Metrics delta = right - left Terms section lists predictors lost going full reduced: log(food) disappears mu submodel temperature disappears sigma submodel. Metrics section quantifies cost: full model uses df pays back log-likelihood; AIC BIC pick model balances two. delta = right - left, sign tells fit AIC prefers: negative delta means right fit (, reduced model) lower — better — AIC; positive delta means left fit (full model) . Read sign delta column read magnitude. Takeaway. data, family — pass metrics = TRUE read delta column model selection top structural diff.
code: library(symbolizer) library(drmTMB) #>  #> Attaching package: 'drmTMB' #> The following object is masked from 'package:base': #>  #>     beta  set.seed(20260524) n <- 200 dat <- data.frame(   temperature = runif(n, 8, 30),   food        = rlnorm(n, 1.5, 0.6) ) dat$body_mass <- with(dat,   rnorm(n, 5 + 0.5 * temperature + 2 * log(food), 2) )  fit_full <- drmTMB(   drm_formula(body_mass ~ temperature + log(food),               sigma     ~ temperature),   family = gaussian(), data = dat ) fit_reduced <- drmTMB(   drm_formula(body_mass ~ temperature, sigma ~ 1),   family = gaussian(), data = dat )  sym_full    <- symbolize(fit_full) sym_reduced <- symbolize(fit_reduced) cmp1 <- compare_symbolic(sym_full, sym_reduced, metrics = TRUE) cmp1

code: set.seed(7L) n2 <- 150 dat2 <- data.frame(   body_mass   = rnorm(n2, 30, 2),   temperature = runif(n2, 10, 25),   site        = factor(rep(letters[1:6], length.out = n2)) )  fit_noRE <- drmTMB(   drm_formula(body_mass ~ temperature, sigma ~ 1),   family = gaussian(), data = dat2 ) fit_RE <- drmTMB(   drm_formula(body_mass ~ temperature + (1 | site), sigma ~ 1),   family = gaussian(), data = dat2 )  sym_noRE <- symbolize(fit_noRE) sym_RE   <- symbolize(fit_RE)  cmp2 <- compare_symbolic(sym_noRE, sym_RE, metrics = TRUE) cmp2

what: 4. Worked example 3: univariate versus bivariate Gaussian
title: Comparing two symbolized models
text: Sometimes two fits aren’t scale . univariate Gaussian fit predicts one response; bivariate Gaussian fit predicts two responses jointly. structural diff still works — metrics refuse compute deltas, clear note. Model summaries Submodels Terms Assumptions Metrics Deltas computed: incomparable: family differs (left = gaussian, right = biv_gaussian) Submodels block shows structural extension cleanly: univariate’s mu, sigma left_only; bivariate’s mu1, mu2, sigma1, sigma2, rho12 right_only. None submodel names differ. Metrics block shows raw AIC, BIC, logLik, df side transparency — delta column NA print output flags “deltas computed: incomparable: family differs (left = gaussian, right = biv_gaussian)”. ’s deliberate. two likelihoods aren’t scale: univariate fit sum n univariate Gaussian densities, bivariate fit sum n bivariate joint densities. Comparing AIC values directly misleading. Takeaway. compare_symbolic works structurally regardless whether two fits comparable likelihood scale. metrics = TRUE honest: refuses compute deltas fits aren’t comparable, tells .
code: set.seed(20260524) n3 <- 80 e1 <- rnorm(n3); e2 <- 0.6 * e1 + sqrt(1 - 0.6^2) * rnorm(n3) dat3 <- data.frame(   growth = 30 + 1.5 * rnorm(n3) + e1,   repro  = 10 + 0.8 * rnorm(n3) + e2,   x1 = rnorm(n3), x2 = rnorm(n3) )  fit_uv <- drmTMB(   drm_formula(growth ~ x1, sigma ~ 1),   family = gaussian(), data = dat3 ) fit_bv <- drmTMB(   drm_formula(mu1 = growth ~ x1, mu2 = repro ~ x2,               sigma1 = ~ 1, sigma2 = ~ 1, rho12 = ~ 1),   family = biv_gaussian(), data = dat3 )  sym_uv <- symbolize(fit_uv) sym_bv <- symbolize(fit_bv)  cmp3 <- compare_symbolic(sym_uv, sym_bv, metrics = TRUE) cmp3

what: 1. Why distributional models need a structured story
title: Understanding a drmTMB fit with symbolizer
text: drmTMB fits Gaussian location-scale models, bivariate Gaussian location-scale-correlation models, family non-Gaussian distributional models (Student-t, lognormal, Gamma, beta, beta-binomial, Poisson, nbinom2, truncated nbinom2, optional zero-inflation / hurdle / cumulative-logit components). univariate location-scale fit two linear predictors: one mean mu, one residual standard deviation sigma. depend covariates. link function. coefficient vector. structure makes question fit actually say? genuinely hard answer one line. mean coefficient temperature lives response scale. sigma coefficient temperature lives log scale. residual SD longer single number; vector one entry per observation. reader sees summary(fit) keep head reading table. symbolizer returns symbolized_model: structured object connects R formula symbolic equation, assumptions, per-coefficient readings every relevant scale, short list diagnostic next steps. Every renderer package consumes object. prose generated language model runtime; every phrase comes template inst/extdata/. Takeaway. drmTMB fit structure single regression table. symbolized_model read instead holding head.

title: Understanding a drmTMB fit with symbolizer
text: small fit, way example. body_mass depends temperature submodels: two arguments drm_formula() map directly two linear predictors. body_mass ~ temperature defines mu submodel; sigma ~ temperature defines sigma submodel. symbolize() reads fit returns structured object: equations(sym) exposes model one row per renderable block. notation = "" argument controls result prints; notations always live object. Index form: \begin{aligned} W_i \mid \mu_i,\, \sigma_i \sim \mathrm{Normal}(\mu_i,\, \sigma_i^2) \\ \mu_i = \beta_{0} + \beta_{1} \, T_i \\ \log(\sigma_i) = \gamma_{0} + \gamma_{1} \, T_i \end{aligned} Matrix form: \begin{aligned} \mathbf{w} \mid \boldsymbol{\mu},\, \boldsymbol{\sigma} \sim \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu},\, \mathrm{diag}(\boldsymbol{\sigma}^2)) \\ \boldsymbol{\mu} = \mathbf{X} \boldsymbol{\beta} \\ \log(\boldsymbol{\sigma}) = \mathbf{X}_{\sigma} \boldsymbol{\gamma} \end{aligned} math, index form W_i \mid \mu_i,\, \sigma_i \sim \mathrm{Normal}(\mu_i,\, \sigma_i^2), \mu_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1\, T_i, \qquad \log(\sigma_i) = \gamma_0 + \gamma_1\, T_i, matrix form \mathbf{w} \mid \boldsymbol{\mu},\, \boldsymbol{\sigma}   \sim \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu},\, \mathrm{diag}(\boldsymbol{\sigma}^2)), \boldsymbol{\mu} = \mathbf{X}\,\boldsymbol{\beta}, \qquad   \log(\boldsymbol{\sigma}) = \mathbf{Z}\,\boldsymbol{\gamma}. piece R call produced one piece math. left half drm_formula() (body_mass ~ temperature) became mu line; right half (sigma ~ temperature) became log-sigma line; family = gaussian() choice became distribution line pinned identity link mu. Takeaway. argument drm_formula() produces one line math. mapping one--one; nothing implicit.
code: library(symbolizer) library(drmTMB) #>  #> Attaching package: 'drmTMB' #> The following object is masked from 'package:base': #>  #>     beta  set.seed(20260523) n <- 120 temperature <- runif(n, 10, 25) dat <- data.frame(   body_mass   = rnorm(n, 30 + 0.4 * temperature, exp(0.5 + 0.08 * temperature)),   temperature = temperature )  fit <- drmTMB(   drm_formula(body_mass ~ temperature, sigma ~ temperature),   family = gaussian(),   data   = dat ) sym <- symbolize(   fit,   symbols = c(body_mass = "W_i", temperature = "T_i"),   units   = c(body_mass = "g",   temperature = "C"),   context = "Gaussian location-scale body-size fit" ) equations(sym, notation = "both")

what: 3. What sigma means in a location-scale model
title: Understanding a drmTMB fit with symbolizer
text: introductory regression, sigma scalar — residual SD, estimated whole dataset. drmTMB location-scale fit vector: observation predicted SD, given linear predictor log scale. choice cosmetic. changes units every coefficient sigma submodel. drmTMB locks log link sigma, \log(\sigma_i) = \gamma_0 + \gamma_1 T_i \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad   \sigma_i = \exp(\gamma_0)\,\exp(\gamma_1 T_i). Two readings follow. \gamma_0 \log(\sigma) reference (, T_i = 0). \exp(\gamma_0) residual SD reference value. \gamma_1 change \log(\sigma) per one-unit change temperature. biological reading multiplicative: one-unit change temperature multiplies residual SD \exp(\gamma_1). \gamma_1 > 0, hotter sites variable; \gamma_1 < 0, less variable. parameter_interpretation() reads coefficient every relevant scale : Rows marked * 95% confidence interval excludes zero (CI method: wald). variance_scale_reading column one work sigma coefficients: states multiplicative effect residual SD , fitted value \exp(\hat{\gamma}_1) already substituted . Takeaway. observation predicted sigma. sigma coefficients live log scale; exp() slope multiplicative factor residual SD.

what: 5. Random intercepts and the assumption swap
title: Understanding a drmTMB fit with symbolizer
text: random intercept enters mu submodel, independence statement automatically updates. symbolizer swaps unconditional “observations conditionally independent given predictors” row conditional “observations conditionally independent given predictors random effects” row. small fit demonstrates: mu equation picks + u_{\mathrm{site}()} term, new random-effect distribution row appears equation block: Index form: \begin{aligned} W_i \mid \mu_i,\, \sigma_i \sim \mathrm{Normal}(\mu_i,\, \sigma_i^2) \\ \mu_i = \beta_{0} + \beta_{1} \, T_i + u_{site()} \\ \log(\sigma_i) = \gamma_{0} + \gamma_{1} \, T_i \\ u_{site} \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\, \sigma_{site}^2) \end{aligned} Matrix form: \begin{aligned} \mathbf{w} \mid \boldsymbol{\mu},\, \boldsymbol{\sigma} \sim \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu},\, \mathrm{diag}(\boldsymbol{\sigma}^2)) \\ \boldsymbol{\mu} = \mathbf{X} \boldsymbol{\beta} + \mathbf{u} \\ \log(\boldsymbol{\sigma}) = \mathbf{X}_{\sigma} \boldsymbol{\gamma} \\ \mathbf{u}_{site} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\, \sigma_{site}^2 \mathbf{}_{6}) \end{aligned} assumption table swaps independence row. code: set.seed(20260523) nr           <- 200 temperature  <- runif(nr, 8, 30) food         <- rlnorm(nr, meanlog = 1.5, sdlog = 0.6) sex          <- factor(sample(c("female", "male"), nr, replace = TRUE)) site         <- factor(sample(letters[1:8], nr, replace = TRUE))  site_re <- rnorm(8, sd = 1.5) mu_r    <- 5 + 0.5 * temperature + 2 * log(food) +              3 * (sex == "male") + site_re[site] sg_r    <- exp(0.3 + 0.05 * temperature + 0.1 * (sex == "male")) dat_r   <- data.frame(   body_mass = rnorm(nr, mu_r, sg_r),   temperature = temperature, food = food, sex = sex, site = site )  fit_rich <- drmTMB(   drm_formula(     body_mass ~ temperature + log(food) + sex + (1 | site),     sigma ~ temperature + sex   ),   family = gaussian(),   data   = dat_r ) sym_rich <- symbolize(   fit_rich,   symbols = c(body_mass = "W_i", temperature = "T_i",               food      = "F_i", sex         = "S_i"),   units   = c(body_mass = "g",   temperature = "C", food = "g/day"),   context = "structured body-size location-scale model" ) formula_bridge(sym_rich) notation_bridge(sym_rich)

what: 7. Two responses at once: bivariate Gaussian
title: Understanding a drmTMB fit with symbolizer
text: measure two responses subject — paired growth reproduction, two morphometric traits, behaviour physiological correlate — univariate fit fits response isolation ignores residual correlation . drmTMB’s biv_gaussian() family models responses jointly, residual correlation \rho_{12} can depend covariates. symbolized_model carries five submodels instead two. appears formula_bridge() R syntax, statistical meaning, symbolic form: mu1, mu2 two mean predictors; sigma1, sigma2 two log-SD predictors (one residual SD per response); rho12 residual correlation Fisher-z scale (linear predictor can range \mathbb{R} correlation stays (-1, 1)). joint conditional distribution rendered index matrix forms: Index form: \begin{aligned} (Y_{1i}, Y_{2i}) \mid \mu_{1i},\, \mu_{2i},\, \sigma_{1i},\, \sigma_{2i},\, \rho_{12,} \sim \mathcal{N}_2\!\left((\mu_{1i}, \mu_{2i}),\, \Sigma_i\right) \\ \mu_{1i} = \beta_{1,0} + \beta_{1,1} \, \mathrm{x1}_i \\ \mu_{2i} = \beta_{2,0} + \beta_{2,1} \, \mathrm{x2}_i \\ \log(\sigma_{1i}) = \gamma_{1,0} \\ \log(\sigma_{2i}) = \gamma_{2,0} \\ \mathrm{tanh}^{-1}(\rho_{12,}) = \rho_{0} \\ \Sigma_i = \begin{pmatrix}\sigma_{1i}^2 & \rho_{12,}\sigma_{1i}\sigma_{2i} \\ \rho_{12,}\sigma_{1i}\sigma_{2i} & \sigma_{2i}^2\end{pmatrix} \end{aligned} Matrix form: \begin{aligned} \mathbf{Y} \mid \mathbf{M},\, \mathbf{S},\, \boldsymbol{\rho}_{12} \sim \mathcal{N}_2(\mathbf{M},\, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}) \\ \boldsymbol{\mu}_{1} = \mathbf{X}_{1} \boldsymbol{\beta}_{1} \\ \boldsymbol{\mu}_{2} = \mathbf{X}_{2} \boldsymbol{\beta}_{2} \\ \log(\boldsymbol{\sigma}_{1}) = \mathbf{X}_{\sigma_{1}} \boldsymbol{\gamma}_{1} \\ \log(\boldsymbol{\sigma}_{2}) = \mathbf{X}_{\sigma_{2}} \boldsymbol{\gamma}_{2} \\ \mathrm{tanh}^{-1}(\boldsymbol{\rho}_{12}) = \mathbf{W} \boldsymbol{\rho} \\ \boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \mathrm{diag}(\boldsymbol{\sigma}_{1}) \mathbf{R}(\boldsymbol{\rho}_{12}) \mathrm{diag}(\boldsymbol{\sigma}_{2}) \end{aligned} matrix form cleaner reading: \mathbf{Y} n \times 2 response matrix, \mathbf{M} stacks per-observation mean vectors, \boldsymbol{\Sigma} per-observation 2 \times 2 covariance matrix \sigma_{1,}\,\sigma_{2,}\,\rho_{12,} -diagonal. rho12 coefficient gets multi-scale treatment every coefficient. reading row points reader Fisher-z scale (coefficient lives), natural correlation scale (tanh() link), biological meaning (residual co-variation two responses): Rows marked * 95% confidence interval excludes zero (CI method: wald). Takeaway. symbolized_model interface scales two submodels five. formula_bridge shows new submodels, joint distribution exposes \boldsymbol{\Sigma}, parameter_interpretation gives rho12 row multi-scale reading every coefficient.
code: set.seed(20260524) nb <- 80 x1 <- rnorm(nb) x2 <- rnorm(nb) # Cholesky factorisation for two correlated standard normals (rho = 0.6), # no extra package needed: e1 <- rnorm(nb) e2 <- 0.6 * e1 + sqrt(1 - 0.6^2) * rnorm(nb) dat_biv <- data.frame(   growth = 30 + 1.5 * x1 + e1,   repro  = 10 + 0.8 * x2 + e2,   x1     = x1,   x2     = x2 )  fit_biv <- drmTMB(   drm_formula(     mu1    = growth ~ x1,     mu2    = repro  ~ x2,     sigma1 = ~ 1,     sigma2 = ~ 1,     rho12  = ~ 1   ),   family = biv_gaussian(),   data   = dat_biv )  sym_biv <- symbolize(fit_biv) formula_bridge(sym_biv) equations(sym_biv, notation = "both") rho_rows <- parameter_interpretation(sym_biv) rho_rows[rho_rows$submodel == "rho12", ]

text: Step 3 forced male female regression lines parallel. Adding interaction lets different slopes: sex * body_size expands sex + body_size + sex:body_size. design matrix gains fourth column interaction: Four columns: (Intercept), sexmale, body_size, sexmale:body_size. interaction column product sexmale dummy continuous body_size — zero every female (sexmale dummy zero), equals body_size every male. coefficient table: Four coefficients read. Let us call \beta_0 (intercept), \beta_1 (sexmale), \beta_2 (body_size), \beta_3 (sexmale:body_size). model \mathrm{E}(W_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot \mathrm{male}_i + \beta_2 \cdot L_i + \beta_3 \cdot \mathrm{male}_i \cdot L_i. title: Reading factors, dummies, and interactions
text: six steps cover mechanics. six pitfalls cover readings — every one sentence heard biologist say loud fit. pitfall structure: Symptom (goes wrong), Diagnosis (), code block showing wrong reading right one, one-sentence Rule thumb carry away.

previous_headings: Common pitfalls
what: Pitfall 1: The intercept is not “the average response”
title: Reading factors, dummies, and interactions
text: Symptom. reviewer asks intercept means; author answers “average body mass”. number way compared mean(dat$body_mass), now everyone confused. Diagnosis. body_mass ~ sex + body_size, intercept expected response reference level every factor zero every continuous predictor. fit sex = factor(female, male) means “expected body_mass FEMALE body_size = 0”. overall mean unless sexes balanced body_size already centred zero. Rule thumb. Read intercept expected response reference factor level zero every continuous predictor.
code: n_p1 <- 80 sex_p1 <- factor(sample(c("female", "male"), n_p1, replace = TRUE)) bs_p1  <- runif(n_p1, 50, 150) dat_p1 <- data.frame(   body_mass = rnorm(n_p1, 30 + 5 * (sex_p1 == "male") + 0.2 * bs_p1, 3),   sex       = sex_p1,   body_size = bs_p1 ) fit_p1 <- drmTMB(   drm_formula(body_mass ~ sex + body_size, sigma ~ 1),   family = gaussian(), data = dat_p1 ) sym_p1 <- symbolize(fit_p1, context = "intercept reading")  # WRONG: read the intercept as the grand mean. #   "the average body mass is 12.0 g" -- it is not. # RIGHT: read the intercept as the reference cell. #   symbol_table() flags the reference level so this is auditable. symbol_table(sym_p1)

previous_headings: Common pitfalls
what: Pitfall 2: A factor contrast is not the group’s mean
title: Reading factors, dummies, and interactions
text: Symptom. paper sentence says “male body mass 5 g (sexmale coefficient)”. reader checks mean(body_mass[sex == "male"]) gets ~35 g. sentence wrong. Diagnosis. sexmale coefficient difference male female cell means, male mean. male mean (Intercept) + sexmale. group_means(sym, = "sex") returns cell mean directly confidence band, readers actually wanted. Group means Rows marked * 95% confidence interval excludes zero (CI method: wald). Rule thumb. Coefficients factor levels differences reference; use group_means(sym) see group means .
code: n_p2 <- 80 sex_p2 <- factor(sample(c("female", "male"), n_p2, replace = TRUE)) dat_p2 <- data.frame(   body_mass = rnorm(n_p2, 30 + 5 * (sex_p2 == "male"), 3),   sex       = sex_p2 ) fit_p2 <- drmTMB(   drm_formula(body_mass ~ sex, sigma ~ 1),   family = gaussian(), data = dat_p2 ) sym_p2 <- symbolize(fit_p2, context = "contrast vs cell mean")  # WRONG: read the sexmale coefficient as the male mean. sym_p2$fixed_effects[, c("term_label", "estimate")] #> # A tibble: 3 × 2 #>   term_label  estimate #>   <chr>          <dbl> #> 1 (Intercept)    30.0  #> 2 sex             5.35 #> 3 (Intercept)     1.02  # RIGHT: ask for the cell means directly. group_means(sym_p2, by = "sex")

previous_headings: Common pitfalls
what: Pitfall 3: An interaction is not “the effect of A on B”
title: Reading factors, dummies, and interactions
text: Symptom. methods section says “interaction tests whether sex effect body size”. category error — sex effect body size; interaction tests whether slope one predictor depends level . Diagnosis. body_mass ~ sex * body_size, sexmale:body_size coefficient difference male female slopes body_size, “effect sex body_size”. honest reading “slope body_size X females X + Y males”. group_slopes(sym, continuous = "body_size") returns per-group slopes directly. Group slopes body_size Rows marked * 95% confidence interval excludes zero (CI method: wald). Rule thumb. interaction coefficient difference two effects, either effect alone; use group_slopes(sym, continuous = ...) read group’s slope.
code: n_p3 <- 80 sex_p3 <- factor(sample(c("female", "male"), n_p3, replace = TRUE)) bs_p3  <- runif(n_p3, 50, 150) dat_p3 <- data.frame(   body_mass = rnorm(     n_p3,     30 + 5 * (sex_p3 == "male") + 0.2 * bs_p3 +       0.05 * (sex_p3 == "male") * bs_p3,     3   ),   sex       = sex_p3,   body_size = bs_p3 ) fit_p3 <- drmTMB(   drm_formula(body_mass ~ sex * body_size, sigma ~ 1),   family = gaussian(), data = dat_p3 ) sym_p3 <- symbolize(fit_p3, context = "interaction wording")  # WRONG: "the sexmale:body_size coefficient is the effect of sex on body_size." # RIGHT: it is the difference in body_size slopes between male and female. group_slopes(sym_p3, continuous = "body_size")

previous_headings: Common pitfalls
what: Pitfall 4: Wald CIs can be too narrow with few groups
title: Reading factors, dummies, and interactions
text: Symptom. fit (1 | site) six sites reports tight confidence bands fixed effects. bands look precise data justify, reviewer asks computed. Diagnosis. drmTMB’s default ci_method = "wald", uses asymptotic normal approximation. sd(site) estimated handful groups, asymptotic regime kicked , Wald intervals -state precision. Profile-likelihood intervals honest slower compute. flag lives symbolize() choice recorded x$metadata$ci_method propagates every downstream reading. Rule thumb. sd(group) estimated groups, pass ci_method = "profile" symbolize() honest interval.
code: # WRONG: take the default Wald CI when only a few groups inform sd(site). sym_wald <- symbolize(fit, ci_method = "wald")  # RIGHT: ask for a profile CI — slower, but honest. sym_prof <- symbolize(fit, ci_method = "profile")

previous_headings: Common pitfalls
what: Pitfall 5: Dropping the intercept doesn’t always do what you think
title: Reading factors, dummies, and interactions
text: Symptom. user wants every cell mean directly, types y ~ 0 + sex + site thinking give sex × site cell means, surprised coefficients still look like contrasts. Diagnosis. y ~ 0 + sex one factor give cell means directly (one coefficient per level). adding second predictor, e.g. y ~ 0 + sex + site, gives “sex cell means PLUS site contrasts reference site”. non-orthogonality two factors without intercept rarely reader wanted. group_means(sym, = c("sex", "site")) returns every cell mean correctly regardless formula written. Group means Rows marked * 95% confidence interval excludes zero (CI method: wald). Rule thumb. two factors, safest way get cell means group_means(sym, = c(...)), hand-built intercept-less formula.
code: n_p5 <- 100 sex_p5  <- factor(sample(c("female", "male"), n_p5, replace = TRUE)) site_p5 <- factor(sample(c("A", "B", "C"), n_p5, replace = TRUE)) dat_p5 <- data.frame(   body_mass = rnorm(n_p5, 30 + 5 * (sex_p5 == "male"), 3),   sex       = sex_p5,   site      = site_p5 )  # WRONG: drop the intercept and hope to read all 6 cell means off the table. fit_p5_wrong <- drmTMB(   drm_formula(body_mass ~ 0 + sex + site, sigma ~ 1),   family = gaussian(), data = dat_p5 )  # RIGHT: keep the intercept in, fit ~ sex * site, then use group_means(). fit_p5_right <- drmTMB(   drm_formula(body_mass ~ sex * site, sigma ~ 1),   family = gaussian(), data = dat_p5 ) sym_p5 <- symbolize(fit_p5_right, context = "all cell means") group_means(sym_p5, by = c("sex", "site"))

what: Pitfall 6: poly(x, 2) and I(x^2) are not the same
title: Reading factors, dummies, and interactions
text: Symptom. paper reports “slope body_size 0.18 g/mm (poly(body_size, 2)1 coefficient)”. number happens match expected linear slope, looks fine — column first orthogonal polynomial body_size, raw linear term. Diagnosis. poly(x, 2) produces two ORTHOGONAL columns: combination x x^2 scaled two columns uncorrelated. first column “slope x”. contrast (x^2) puts literal x^2 column design matrix alongside separate linear x term, now linear coefficient slope x = 0. two parameterisations carry information coefficient interpretations differ. Use whichever fits story. Rule thumb. Use poly(x, 2) want orthogonal columns (uncorrelated polynomial terms); use (x^2) want literal quadratic interpretation.
code: n_p6 <- 80 bs_p6 <- runif(n_p6, -1, 1) dat_p6 <- data.frame(   body_mass = rnorm(n_p6, 30 + 0.2 * bs_p6 + 0.5 * bs_p6^2, 1),   body_size = bs_p6 )  # WRONG: read the poly() column as a literal linear slope. fit_p6_poly <- drmTMB(   drm_formula(body_mass ~ poly(body_size, 2), sigma ~ 1),   family = gaussian(), data = dat_p6 ) sym_p6_poly <- symbolize(fit_p6_poly, context = "orthogonal polynomial")  # RIGHT: use I(x^2) when you want a literal quadratic reading. fit_p6_raw <- drmTMB(   drm_formula(body_mass ~ body_size + I(body_size^2), sigma ~ 1),   family = gaussian(), data = dat_p6 ) sym_p6_raw <- symbolize(fit_p6_raw, context = "raw quadratic")  symbol_table(sym_p6_poly) symbol_table(sym_p6_raw)

text: Six rules thumb: Continuous, roughly symmetric, fixed scale → gaussian. Continuous, symmetric, heavier tails (outliers tolerated) → student. title: Latent variables in ecology: a gllvmTMB worked example
text: behavioural ecologist measures five traits — boldness novel arena, exploration maze, aggression mirror, activity home cage, time---shelter — forty fish, three times . Two themes keep coming data. Bolder fish also tend exploratory. Active fish tend spend time shelter. also second pattern: individual fish bolder usual given day, tends exploratory aggressive day. first pattern stable differences individuals; second coordinated within-individual fluctuations. literature names separately: Behavioural syndromes (Sih et al. 2004; Dingemanse & Dochtermann 2013): -individual axes organise trait values across population — makes individual ’s boldness reliably predict individual ’s exploration. Integrated plasticity (Dingemanse & Dochtermann 2013; Mathot & Dingemanse 2015): within-individual axes organise trait fluctuations across occasions individual. factor-analytic objects model. output biologist wants two loading matrices (\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_B , \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_W within), per-trait communality tier, per-trait repeatability R_t = (\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_B)_{tt} / [(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_B)_{tt} + (\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_W)_{tt}]. Takeaway. biological question splits two layers: syndromes () integrated plasticity (within). One generalised linear latent-variable model (GLLVM) writes layers one fit.

title: Latent variables in ecology: a gllvmTMB worked example
text: simulate known truth biological reading end can checked. truth puts traits 1-3 first -individual axis (boldness-exploration-aggression syndrome), traits 4-5 second -individual axis (activity-shelter-use syndrome), adds single shared within-individual axis (coordinated state-shift moves five behaviours together across occasions). DGP carries layers: stable -individual structure (\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_B, \boldsymbol{\Psi}_B) coordinated within-individual structure (\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_W, \boldsymbol{\Psi}_W). fit Widget 2 recover . Takeaway. Forty individuals, three sessions , five traits — long format, one row per (individual, session, trait). simulated truth -individual two-axis structure within-individual one-axis structure.
code: library(symbolizer) library(gllvmTMB) library(lme4) #> Loading required package: Matrix #>  #> Attaching package: 'Matrix' #> The following object is masked from 'package:symbolizer': #>  #>     expand  set.seed(20260523) n_ind  <- 40L  # individuals (units) n_sess <- 3L   # repeated sessions per individual n_tr   <- 5L   # traits  # True BETWEEN-individual loading matrix Lambda_B (5 traits x 2 latents). # Traits 1-3 load on axis 1 (the bold-explore-aggress syndrome); traits # 4-5 load on axis 2 (the activity-shelter syndrome). Lam_B <- matrix(c(1.0, 0.0,                   0.7, 0.0,                   0.6, 0.0,                   0.0, 1.0,                   0.0, 0.7),                 nrow = n_tr, ncol = 2L) psi_B <- rep(0.4, n_tr)   # trait-specific between-individual uniqueness SD  # True WITHIN-individual loading vector Lambda_W (5 traits x 1 latent). # A single state-shift axis: when an individual is "up" today, all five # behaviours move together by trait-specific amounts. This is what # integrated-plasticity literature calls a coordinated state. Lam_W <- matrix(c(0.5, 0.3, 0.4, 0.3, 0.4), nrow = n_tr, ncol = 1L) psi_W <- rep(0.2, n_tr)   # trait-specific within-individual uniqueness SD  # Per-individual between-latent scores z_B in R^2 (one per individual). z_B <- matrix(rnorm(n_ind * 2L), nrow = n_ind, ncol = 2L) psi_B_resid <- matrix(rnorm(n_ind * n_tr,                             sd = rep(psi_B, each = n_ind)),                       nrow = n_ind, ncol = n_tr) # Between-individual trait mean (per individual, per trait). mu_ind_trait <- z_B %*% t(Lam_B) + psi_B_resid  # Per-observation within-latent scores z_W in R^1 (one per (ind, sess)). n_obs_per_ind <- n_sess z_W <- matrix(rnorm(n_ind * n_sess), nrow = n_ind * n_sess, ncol = 1L) psi_W_resid <- matrix(rnorm(n_ind * n_sess * n_tr,                             sd = rep(psi_W, each = n_ind * n_sess)),                       nrow = n_ind * n_sess, ncol = n_tr) within_state <- z_W %*% t(Lam_W) + psi_W_resid    # (n_ind * n_sess) x n_tr  # Expand to long-format: one row per (individual, session, trait). Trait # labels are short codes (t1..t5) for the math; their biological readings # from §1 are: #   t1 = boldness          t4 = activity #   t2 = exploration       t5 = time-out-of-shelter #   t3 = aggression dat <- expand.grid(   trait      = factor(paste0("t", seq_len(n_tr)),                       levels = paste0("t", seq_len(n_tr))),   session    = factor(seq_len(n_sess)),   individual = factor(seq_len(n_ind)) ) # Look up the row index in `within_state` for each (individual, session). obs_idx <- as.integer(dat$individual) * n_sess - n_sess +            as.integer(dat$session) dat$value <- mu_ind_trait[cbind(as.integer(dat$individual),                                  as.integer(dat$trait))] +               within_state[cbind(obs_idx,                                   as.integer(dat$trait))] # Stable (individual, session) observation id for the obs-level term. dat$obs <- factor(paste(dat$individual, dat$session, sep = "_")) head(dat, 6) #>   trait session individual      value obs #> 1    t1       1          1  0.5810401 1_1 #> 2    t2       1          1 -0.3152411 1_1 #> 3    t3       1          1 -0.1733318 1_1 #> 4    t4       1          1  0.5749212 1_1 #> 5    t5       1          1  0.3648401 1_1 #> 6    t1       2          1  0.6282983 1_2

what: 3. The univariate root: one trait at a time
title: Latent variables in ecology: a gllvmTMB worked example
text: model five traits jointly, recall univariate mixed model behavioural ecologists already know. one trait y measured N individuals J_i occasions: y_{ij} = \mu + u_i + e_{ij}, \qquad u_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2_u), \qquad e_{ij} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2_e). classical repeatability (Nakagawa & Schielzeth 2010) R = \frac{\sigma^2_u}{\sigma^2_u + \sigma^2_e}. lme4 syntax, fit one trait time: random intercept (1 | individual) captures stable -individual variation; everything else lands residual. repeatability R -individual share total variance — computed trait--trait, ’s univariate readout GLLVM upgrades two structured matrices. Takeaway. Univariate R = \sigma^2_u / (\sigma^2_u + \sigma^2_e) trait--trait readout multivariate model generalises. GLLVM upgrade replaces two scalars two T \times T matrices \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_B, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_W — decomposes factor-analytically.
code: fit_uni <- lmer(value ~ 1 + (1 | individual),                 data = subset(dat, trait == "t1")) vc <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(fit_uni)) vc[, c("grp", "vcov")] #>          grp      vcov #> 1 individual 1.0103895 #> 2   Residual 0.3356346 sigma2_u <- vc$vcov[vc$grp == "individual"] sigma2_e <- vc$vcov[vc$grp == "Residual"] R_t1 <- sigma2_u / (sigma2_u + sigma2_e) cat("Repeatability for t1:", round(R_t1, 3), "\n") #> Repeatability for t1: 0.751

title: Latent variables in ecology: a gllvmTMB worked example
text: fully parameterised multivariate covariance T traits requires T(T+1)/2 free parameters. T = 5 traits one tier ’s 15 parameters; within tiers doubles 30. T = 10 traits per tier ’d need 110 covariance parameters fixed effects enter. Animal-personality studies typically N \approx 40–200 individuals; resulting likelihood flat — convergence unstable standard errors wide enough interpretation becomes risky (McGillycuddy et al. 2025). factor-analytic answer decompose \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_B = \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_B \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_B^{\!\top} + \boldsymbol{\Psi}_B, \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_B \\mathbb{R}^{T \times d_B} reduced-rank loading matrix (d_B \ll T) \boldsymbol{\Psi}_B diagonal trait-specific uniquenesses. parameter count drops T(T+1)/2 T(d_B + 1) - d_B(d_B - 1)/2. T = 5, d_B = 2: 15 \14; T = 10, d_B = 2: 55 \29; T = 10 tiers d_B = d_W = 2: 110 \58. reduction modest T small dramatic T grows. interpretive payoff shape directions. shared loadings \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_B name -individual axes — syndromes. uniquenesses \boldsymbol{\Psi}_B name shared axes explain — trait-specific -individual variance. within-individual tier, \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_W names coordinated states; \boldsymbol{\Psi}_W names trait-specific within-individual residual variance. tiers factor-analytic way; ’s unifying move. Takeaway. Reduced-rank decomposition \boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \boldsymbol{\Lambda}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{\!\top} + \boldsymbol{\Psi} stabilises fit surfaces biology — applies tiers without changing form.

title: Latent variables in ecology: a gllvmTMB worked example
text: model can written two ways. long form matches way gllvmTMB() actually fits data — one row per (individual, occasion, trait) cell, scalar response. wide form matches factor-analytic textbooks — one row per observation, trait-vector response. two panels place side side; decompose tier’s covariance via \boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \boldsymbol{\Lambda}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{\!\top} + \boldsymbol{\Psi}. Bridge. two forms describe model. wide form makes covariance decomposition explicit; long form gllvmTMB() actually fits. Index ranges individuals, j occasions, t traits, k = 1, \ldots, d_B -axes, \ell = 1, \ldots, d_W within-axes. \mu_t trait t grand mean; \lambda_{B,tk} loading trait t -axis k; \lambda_{W,t\ell} loading trait t within-axis \ell; z_{B,ik} individual ’s position -axis k; z_{W,ij\ell} (individual , session j)’s position within-axis \ell; \boldsymbol{\Psi}_B = \mathrm{diag}(\psi_{B,1}^2, \ldots, \psi_{B,T}^2) collects trait-specific -individual uniquenesses; similarly \boldsymbol{\Psi}_W within-individual. Takeaway. Long form one scalar equation per (individual, occasion, trait); wide form one T-vector equation per observation. tier \boldsymbol{\Lambda}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{\!\top} + \boldsymbol{\Psi} decomposition. model, two notations.

title: Building up: from lm to location-scale
text: “truth” ladder gradually uncover: Slope temperature mean: 0.4 g per °C Sex contrast (M − F) mean: +0.7 g Site--site SD mean: 1.5 g Heteroscedasticity: residual SD grows factor exp(0.05) ≈ 1.05 per °C
code: library(symbolizer) set.seed(1)  n <- 200 n_sites <- 12 sites <- factor(rep(paste0("S", sprintf("%02d", seq_len(n_sites))),                     length.out = n)) site_effect <- rnorm(n_sites, 0, 1.5)[as.integer(sites)] sex <- factor(sample(c("F", "M"), n, replace = TRUE)) temperature <- runif(n, 10, 25)  # Mean: linear in temperature, +0.7 for males, plus a site offset. # Variance: heteroscedastic — residual SD grows with temperature. mu_true    <- 30 + 0.4 * temperature + 0.7 * (sex == "M") + site_effect sigma_true <- exp(0.3 + 0.05 * temperature) body_mass  <- rnorm(n, mean = mu_true, sd = sigma_true)  dat <- data.frame(   body_mass   = body_mass,   temperature = temperature,   sex         = sex,   site        = sites ) head(dat, 4) #>   body_mass temperature sex site #> 1  36.82290    23.85953   F  S01 #> 2  32.86767    17.66440   F  S02 #> 3  37.65935    13.86432   M  S03 #> 4  40.17388    10.69691   F  S04

Just temperature mean. equation: \begin{aligned} \mathrm{body\_mass}_i \mid \mu_i,\, \sigma \sim \mathrm{Normal}(\mu_i,\, \sigma^2) \\ \mu_i = \beta_{0} + \beta_{1} \, \mathrm{temperature}_i \end{aligned} symbol dictionary, listing every variable model uses: coefficient means, scale symbolizer knows : Rows marked * 95% confidence interval excludes zero (CI method: wald). far. distribution line response, linear predictor \mu_i, one slope interpret. variance modelling beyond single residual SD. grouping. biological reading “unit change temperature shifts expected body_mass 0.303.”

title: Three flavors of meta-analysis: a cross-package tour
text: Meta-analysis pools K study-level effect sizes y_k, known sampling variance v_k, single summary. idea can tightened three different directions; article walks three side--side across three packages, reader can land whichever combination matches toolkit. Flavor 1 — Traditional random-effects pooling. Studies vary beyond sampling alone explains. headline parameter \tau^2, -study heterogeneity variance: y_k \mid \theta_k \sim \mathcal{N}(\theta_k, v_k), \qquad \theta_k \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \tau^2), \qquad k = 1, \ldots, K. single \tau^2 describes much “true” effect sizes scatter across studies sampling noise accounted . textbook random-effects model (Borenstein et al. 2009; Viechtbauer 2010). Flavor 2 — Phylogenetic meta-analysis. studies related species, -study tier becomes structured phylogeny. total -species variance splits phylogenetic piece (constrained relatedness) non-phylogenetic piece: \theta_k = \mu + u_{p,k} + u_{s,k}, \quad u_p \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \sigma_p^2 \mathbf{}), \quad u_s \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \sigma_s^2 \mathbf{}). \mathbf{} phylogenetic correlation matrix (Cinar et al. 2022; Mizuno et al. 2026). Flavor 3 — Location-scale meta-analysis. moderators predict just mean effect also heterogeneity, scale parameter becomes regression: y_k \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_k, v_k + \tau_k^2), \quad \mu_k = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_k, \quad \log \tau_k = \gamma_0 + \gamma_1 x_k. biological question shifts: moderators predict variable study effects ? — separate mean. Three packages, one math. model can fit metafor, glmmTMB, drmTMB, brms, MCMCglmm. section picks one deep Face (package whose interface cleanly expresses flavor) two light Faces (showing cross-package equivalence reader’s existing fluency carries ). Takeaway. Three flavors, one statistical motivation: separate sampling variance v_k (known per study) heterogeneity \tau^2 (estimated). Phylogenetic location-scale flavors structure heterogeneity .

what: 2. The data: BCG vaccine efficacy trials
title: Three flavors of meta-analysis: a cross-package tour
text: use dat.bcg metafor (Colditz et al. 1994): thirteen randomised trials BCG vaccine tuberculosis, treatment / control case counts per trial. summary effect log risk ratio: y_k = \log\!\left(\frac{a_k / (a_k + b_k)}{c_k / (c_k + d_k)}\right), \qquad v_k = \frac{1}{a_k} - \frac{1}{a_k + b_k} + \frac{1}{c_k} - \frac{1}{c_k + d_k}. Thirteen trials; effect sizes range strong protection (y_k < 0) effect (y_k \approx 0). sampling variances v_k known (computed trial counts) differ across trials — large trials small v_k, small trials large v_k. meta-analysis must respect . Takeaway. effect-size metric (y_k = log RR), known sampling variance metric (v_k). One dataset reused across three flavors .

what: A SEM is a list of regressions
title: Multi-node structural equation models: piecewiseSEM and drmSEM
text: single GLM one response, piecewise SEM several — fitted model, node directed graph. variable predictor one node response another. use keeley data bundled piecewiseSEM: 90 plots California shrubland surveyed wildfire (Grace & Keeley 2006). Five columns appear — stand age, fire severity (firesev), abiotic favourability index (abiotic), plant cover, species richness (rich). simplified slice Grace & Keeley causal backbone posits four directed paths plus one correlated-error arc: firesev ~ age — model treats fire severity response stand age (older stands carry accumulated fuel), cover ~ firesev — plant cover response fire severity, rich ~ abiotic + firesev — richness response abiotic favourability fire severity, rich %~~% cover — richness cover allowed residual covariance (shared unmeasured cause beyond common dependence fire), declared bidirected arc, regression. (arc added illustrate feature; age→firesev→cover/rich paths simplified published backbone.) piecewiseSEM::psem() glues fitted nodes one object. symbolize() reads unit. symbolize() returns symbolized_psem — collator holding one symbolized_model per node (sym$parts), node names declared order (sym$node_names), %~~% arcs (sym$cov_arcs). Every node dispatched class:
code: library(piecewiseSEM) data(keeley)  sem <- psem(   lm(firesev ~ age,              data = keeley),   lm(cover   ~ firesev,          data = keeley),   lm(rich    ~ abiotic + firesev, data = keeley),   rich %~~% cover,   data = keeley ) #> Warning: the 'nobars' function has moved to the reformulas package. Please update your imports, or ask an upstream package maintainer to do so. #> This warning is displayed once per session.  sym <- symbolize(   sem,   symbols = c(firesev = "F_i", cover = "C_i", rich = "R_i",               age = "A_i", abiotic = "B_i") ) sym #> <symbolized_psem>: 3 nodes #>   - firesev (lm, gaussian) #>   - cover (lm, gaussian) #>   - rich (lm, gaussian) #>   1 residual covariance arc: rich ~~ cover sym$node_names #> [1] "firesev" "cover"   "rich" vapply(sym$parts, function(p) p$model$class, character(1)) #> firesev   cover    rich  #>    "lm"    "lm"    "lm"

title: Structural dependence: phylogenetic, animal-model, and spatial random effects
text: phylogenetic dependence Brownian-motion model trait evolution, \mathbf phylogenetic correlation matrix: A_{ij} \;=\; \frac{T_{ij}}{T}, T_{ij} shared branch length species j measured root, T tree height. ultrametric tree tips equidistant root A_{ii} = 1 construction. matrix symmetric positive-definite. Two operational representations exist: two representations encode Brownian-motion prior. tips-version operational default metafor, glmmTMB::propto, brms::gr(cov = ). -nodes version MCMCglmm uses internally (ginverse = list(animal = Ainv)) drmTMB::phylo() builds hood (drmTMB cites Hadfield & Nakagawa 2010 explicitly ?phylo help page). -nodes form richer: gives access ancestral-state BLUPs internal nodes; tips-form marginalises . balanced setup two agree variance estimate \hat\sigma_p^2 — result ’ll return § “Tips-vs -nodes”.
code: suppressPackageStartupMessages({   library(metadat); library(ape); library(metafor); library(MCMCglmm) })  # Real comparative-biology data: Mizuno et al. (2026, Research Synthesis # Methods; tutorial at https://ayumi-495.github.io/phylo_spatial_tutorial/) # use Moura et al. (2021)'s assortative-mating dataset for the phylogenetic # example. dat.moura2021 carries 1,828 Pearson correlations (size-size # assortative mating) across 341 species, plus a phylogeny. We follow the # Mizuno workflow: compute Fisher-z effect sizes via metafor::escalc, # subsample 60 species (each with at least 2 effect sizes for stable # aggregation), and aggregate to one mean Fisher-z per species so the # example is a clean phylogenetic random-intercept model on a Gaussian # trait. The full multilevel-meta-analytic structure (effect-size + # study + species_phylo + species_nonphylo random effects) is the # v0.22 article's topic. data(dat.moura2021, package = "metadat") moura_es <- escalc(measure = "ZCOR", ri = ri, ni = ni,                    data = dat.moura2021$dat)  # Tree tip labels carry Open Tree of Life format ("Genus_species_ottNNN"); # strip the suffix and convert underscores to spaces to match dat$species # ("Genus species"). Drop node labels (duplicated in the source tree; # MCMCglmm::inverseA rejects them otherwise). tree_raw <- dat.moura2021$tree tree_raw$tip.label <- gsub("_", " ", sub("_ott[0-9]+$", "", tree_raw$tip.label)) tree_raw$node.label <- NULL  n_per_sp <- table(moura_es$species) sp_pool  <- intersect(tree_raw$tip.label,                       names(n_per_sp[n_per_sp >= 2L])) set.seed(1) sp_keep  <- sample(sp_pool, 60L)  # Aggregate to one mean Zr per species + variance-of-the-mean for V. agg <- aggregate(cbind(yi, vi) ~ species,                  data = moura_es[moura_es$species %in% sp_keep, ],                  FUN  = function(v) c(mean = mean(v), n = length(v))) dat <- data.frame(   species = factor(as.character(agg$species), levels = sp_keep),   Zr      = agg$yi[, "mean"],   vi      = (agg$vi[, "mean"] * agg$yi[, "n"]) / agg$yi[, "n"]^2,   n_eff   = agg$yi[, "n"] )  tree   <- keep.tip(tree_raw, sp_keep) # Ultrametricise the tree once, here, so every downstream phylogenetic # fit is on the SAME ultrametric tree. Brownian-motion on tips-only A # requires equal root-to-tip distances by construction (A_ii = 1 only # when tips are equidistant from the root); metafor / MCMCglmm / brms / # glmmTMB accept a non-ultrametric tree silently but the BM prior is # then misspecified. drmTMB ENFORCES ultrametricity (it errors otherwise), # which surfaces the assumption that the other packages let pass. The # Moura tree comes from Open Tree of Life with mixed-source branch # lengths, so we smooth it with ape::chronos() (penalised-likelihood # molecular-clock estimate; lambda = 1 = smoothest plausible clock). tree   <- ape::chronos(tree, lambda = 1, quiet = TRUE) class(tree) <- "phylo" A_tips <- vcv.phylo(tree, corr = TRUE) # Reorder A_tips rows/cols to match `sp_keep` (a random sample). Without # this, A_tips inherits the depth-first tree-tip order, so head 5x5 # clusters closely-related species (all passerines, all ~0.85+) and # hides the structural-dependence "mix of relatedness" the widget is # meant to demonstrate. Florence-audit 2026-05-26. A_tips <- A_tips[sp_keep, sp_keep] # Representation 2 -- all-nodes A-inverse (tips + internal nodes, sparse # precision; Hadfield & Nakagawa 2010). With the tree now ultrametric, # scale = TRUE works cleanly (normalises total tree depth to 1, the # canonical BM-prior parameterisation). A_all  <- inverseA(tree, nodes = "ALL", scale = TRUE)  cat("species k =", nrow(dat),     "  Zr range = [", round(min(dat$Zr), 2), ",", round(max(dat$Zr), 2), "]\n") #> species k = 60   Zr range = [ -0.14 , 1.59 ] cat("A off-diagonal quantiles (25/50/75/99%): ",     paste(round(quantile(A_tips[upper.tri(A_tips)], c(.25,.5,.75,.99)), 3),           collapse = " / "), "\n") #> A off-diagonal quantiles (25/50/75/99%):  0 / 0.095 / 0.228 / 0.866

title: Structural dependence: phylogenetic, animal-model, and spatial random effects
text: phylolm (Ho & Ané 2014) fits conceptual model marginalised form: instead writing y = \beta_0 + u_p + e two separate variance components, phylolm absorbs u_p residual give \mathrm{Zr}_i \;=\; \beta_0 + e'_i,\quad \mathbf e' \sim \mathcal N(\mathbf 0,\; \sigma^2\,\mathbf C(\alpha)) \mathbf C(\alpha) tree-derived correlation matrix. Pagel’s \lambda model connection RE form precise: \mathbf C(\lambda) = \lambda\,\mathbf + (1 - \lambda)\,\mathbf , \qquad \sigma_p^2 = \lambda\,\sigma^2, \qquad \sigma_e^2 = (1 - \lambda)\,\sigma^2. \lambda = \sigma_p^2 / (\sigma_p^2 + \sigma_e^2) — phylogenetic heritability H^2 § “Animal-model unification” — two parameterisations agree every prediction. phylolm’s advantage speed: closed-form ML fit fraction second instead Stan’s compile + sample. bridge RE form: take estimated \hat\sigma^2 \hat\lambda summary , \hat\sigma_p^2 = \hat\lambda\,\hat\sigma^2 \hat\sigma_e^2 = (1-\hat\lambda)\,\hat\sigma^2. dataset, reconciled values agree MCMCglmm estimates phylogenetic variance within couple percent, residual variance \sigma_e^2 can differ 20–30 % across three packages — variance split weakly identified one observation per species (see § “unification breaks: identifiability” ). total \hat\sigma_p^2 + \hat\sigma_e^2 heritability \hat H^2 = \hat\lambda stable either component . cross-package agreement story point: every fit attaches conceptual object — phylogenetic correlation matrix \mathbf — even though syntactic surface differs (RE bar MCMCglmm brms, marginalised residual covariance phylolm). RE-form fits (MCMCglmm, brms) report metadata$detected_signals = "phylo"; phylolm reports "phylo_marginal", marginal-form variant phylogenetic signal (absorbs u_p residual, separate u_p tier label). Either way symbolizer attaches symbol-dictionary row \mathbf gates matching phylogenetic assumption rows, matter parameterisation fitted model.

title: Where the variation lives: ICC and repeatability
text: Suppose boldness scored three times 30 individuals, assay temperature recorded time. want repeatability boldness: much variation consistent differences individuals, versus variation within individual across repeats. variance_partition() shows variation lives – one row per source, share total: variation live? variation lives – row one variance component (shown share total single total variance defined). icc() turns single repeatability number. Gaussian-identity fit one random intercept, ICC true proportion variance observed response – data scale: ICC (data scale): 0.694. Data-scale ICC: share total variance lies groups – genuine proportion variance. Takeaway. tenths boldness variation consistent individuals; rest within-individual. -individual share repeatability boldness.
code: set.seed(1) n_ind <- 30L; n_rep <- 3L ind   <- factor(rep(seq_len(n_ind), each = n_rep)) temp  <- round(runif(n_ind * n_rep, 14, 24), 1) u_ind <- rnorm(n_ind, sd = 1.2)                      # between-individual boldness <- 2 + 0.10 * temp + u_ind[ind] + rnorm(n_ind * n_rep, sd = 1.0) dat_g <- data.frame(boldness, temp, ind)  fit_g <- lme4::lmer(boldness ~ temp + (1 | ind), data = dat_g) sym_g <- symbolize(fit_g) variance_partition(sym_g) icc(sym_g)

title: Where the variation lives: ICC and repeatability
text: Now binary outcome: whether offspring survived, several offspring per nest. “repeatability survival across nests” binomial GLMM (1 | nest) random intercept. binomial model residual variance observed 0/1 scale. model lives latent (logit) scale, residual variance known constant \pi^2/3. icc() reports latent-scale ICC, labels – caption keeps honest: ICC (latent scale): 0.116. Latent-scale ICC: proportion variance observed outcome – repeatability link (latent) scale. exactly rptR’s link-scale (.k.. latent-scale) repeatability. repeatability underlying propensity survive, proportion variance realized 0/1 outcome. symbolizer refuses pretend otherwise. Takeaway. Proportion binary data get repeatability – latent scale, residual fixed \pi^2/3 (logit) 1 (probit).
code: set.seed(2) n_nest <- 25L; brood <- 5L nest   <- factor(rep(seq_len(n_nest), each = brood)) temp_n <- round(runif(n_nest * brood, 14, 24), 1) u_nest <- rnorm(n_nest, sd = 1.0)                    # between-nest, logit scale eta    <- -0.2 + 0.05 * temp_n + u_nest[nest] surv   <- rbinom(n_nest * brood, size = 1, prob = plogis(eta)) dat_b  <- data.frame(surv, temp_n, nest)  fit_b <- lme4::glmer(surv ~ temp_n + (1 | nest), data = dat_b,                      family = binomial) sym_b <- symbolize(fit_b) icc(sym_b)

text: §1 Biological question – now names syndromes (-individual) integrated plasticity (within-individual) front. §2 Data – 40 individuals × 3 sessions × 5 traits simulated truth carrying Lambda_B (5×2) Lambda_W (5×1). §3 NEW – univariate motivation via lme4::lmer; classical repeatability R = \sigma^2_u / (\sigma^2_u + \sigma^2_e) (Nakagawa & Schielzeth 2010). §4 NEW – factor-analytic motivation: T(T+1)/2 vs T(d+1) - d(d-1)/2 parameter counting. §5 model symbols – long form / wide form, tiers explicit. §6 Widget 1 – behavioural syndromes (\Sigma_B ). §7 Widget 2 – adds integrated plasticity (\Sigma_W). Documents gllvmTMB’s \sigma_\varepsilon auto-suppression unique(0 + trait | obs) present. §8 Reading biologically – c^2 + \psi^* per tier, R_t per-trait, phenotypic-correlation decomposition r_P = r_B\sqrt{R_t R_m} + r_W\sqrt{(1-R_t)(1-R_m)} (Dingemanse & Dochtermann 2013). §9 Identifiability – rotation, sign, \sigma_\varepsilon auto-suppression expected behaviour. §10 NEW – glmmTMB bridge: latent()/unique() ↔︎ rr()/diag() syntax equivalence readers Nakagawa et al. paper see math. §11 Capability list – updated reflect v0.21.6-redo.

README.Rmd capability matrix roadmap updated reflect v0.4 (zi / hu / cumulative_logit), v0.5 (gllvmTMB binomial), v0.6 (as_dag()), v0.7 (glmmTMB) — previously stopped v0.3.

title: symbolizer 0.7.0
text: New: symbolize.glmmTMB() (first slice). Builds symbolized_model glmmTMB fit Gaussian conditional submodel (identity link), optional (1 | g) random intercepts optional dispformula = ~ z distributional sigma submodel. Non-Gaussian families zero-inflation routed capability registry “Planned reserved” now. new extractor reuses prose layer (assumption / interpretation / symbol-dictionary / formula-bridge builders) producing tibble shapes symbolize.drmTMB(). Family-keyed CSVs inst/extdata/ drive prose, Gaussian glmmTMB fit produces teachable readings drmTMB equivalent. Confidence intervals come glmmTMB::confint(fit, parm = "beta_", method = ci_method). Default ci_method = "wald"; "profile" "uniroot" available.

title: symbolizer 0.7.0
text: parameter_interpretation(sym, scale = ...) now carries confidence-band columns (std_error, confint_low, confint_high, excludes_zero, ci_method) every scale, just scale = "". Previously dropped user picked specific scale, rendered Markdown / pkgdown table omitted CI band even though underlying interpretation tibble .

title: symbolizer 0.6.0
text: New: as_dag(sym) returns structural DAG fitted model three slots: nodes (tibble — response, parameters, predictors, groups, random effects), edges (tibble — predictor→parameter edges, parameter→response distribution edges, group→random-effect edges, random-effect→parameter contributions), dot (single GraphViz / DOT-language string). S3 class symbolic_dag. print() summarises node edge counts emits DOT string copy/paste pointer GraphvizOnline; knit_print() wraps DOT inside fenced dot code block Quarto / Markdown engines support DOT rendering pick automatically. response → double circle, salmon fill parameter (μ, σ, ν, …) → ellipse, cream fill predictor → box, green fill group variable → house shape, lavender fill random effect → circle, orange fill Edges styled relationship: distribution edges bold red; linear-predictor edges solid; group / random-contribution edges dashed. new hard dependencies. render DAG live: paste $dot string https://dreampuf.github.io/GraphvizOnline/, pass DiagrammeR::grViz() (DiagrammeR symbolizer dependency).

what: v0.5 — gllvmTMB binomial (first non-Gaussian latent-variable family)
title: symbolizer 0.5.0
text: symbolize.gllvmTMB() now reads binomial latent-variable models end--end. conditional distribution renders y_{ij} | mu_{t(j)}, Lambda_B, z_{B,} ~ Bernoulli(logit^{-1}(mu_{t(j)} + (Lambda_B z_{B,})_{t(j)})), trait intercepts read logit baseline success probabilities (e.g. “plogis(mu_t)”), loadings Lambda_B noted living logit scale (odds-ratio per unit z). glm_build_distribution() assumption / interpretation template lookups now family-aware: gllvm family slug (gllvm_gaussian, gllvm_binomial, …) selects rows. Added gllvm_template_family() helper maps upstream family name slug. sigma_eps capability check now fires Gaussian gllvm fits. drmTMB’s binomial / Poisson / etc. carry placeholder fit$report$sigma_eps previously triggered spurious capability error. Capability rows flipped First slice gllvmTMB / binomial / mu, Lambda_B, Sigma_B, Psi_B. gllvm families (Poisson, nbinom2, Gamma, lognormal, ordinal, …) stay Planned reserved. pattern now straightforward: add CSV slug, mirror gllvm_gaussian rows family-appropriate wording, add branch glm_build_distribution().

title: symbolizer 0.4.0
text: cumulative_logit — ordered categorical response, proportional-odds model. conditional distribution renders P(Y_i ≤ k | X_i) = logit⁻¹(θ_k − X_i'β) K−1 thresholds replacing intercept. mu linear predictor rendered without intercept term (drmTMB suppresses ; symbolizer matches). Three new assumption rows (proportional_odds, ordered_categorical_response, thresholds_ordered) make PO assumption explicit stay-honest ’s responsible. zi (zero-inflation) submodel layered Poisson nbinom2. Rendered additional zi_linear_predictor component logit(π_zi,) = α₀ + ..., interpretation rows reading α coefficients log-odds structural zero. conditional-distribution assumption row spells mixture P(Y=0) = π_zi + (1−π_zi)·f(0|μ,...). hu (hurdle) submodel layered truncated_nbinom2. shape zi δ coefficients, assumption row reads two-part mixture (P(Y=0) = π_hu; P(Y=k | Y>0) = NegBin⁺(k; μ, exp(σ))). drm_param_index_form() now handles non-digit subscripts cleanly: π_{zi} becomes π_{zi, } rather malformed π_{zi}_i. latent bug surfaced zi/hu submodels started using subscripted Greek symbols.

what: v0.3.2 — two more families, families-tour vignette, README refresh
title: symbolizer 0.4.0
text: beta_binomial (drmTMB::beta_binomial()) — overdispersed binomial counts. Response specified cbind(successes, failures); mean success probability via logit link, precision (inverse-overdispersion) via log link. Coefficients mu read odds ratios; methods_text paragraph names trial count requirement. truncated_nbinom2 (drmTMB::truncated_nbinom2()) — zero-truncated counts. distribution latex flags truncation via \mathrm{NegBin}^{+} support y {1, 2, 3, ...}. methods_text assumption rows explicit mu mean underlying untruncated distribution; observed mean larger. methods_text univariate-family list grows include new families response / sigma / RE substitutions fire without [unfilled: ...] markers. New vignette symbolizer-families — tour seven non- Gaussian families currently shipping. One small fit one key surface per family (distribution latex, biological reading mu, methods_text excerpt), plus six rules thumb picking family. Bivariate Gaussian cross-referenced rather repeated since section drmTMB tour.

what: v0.3.1 — random slopes, response-scale group_means, bigger hex
title: symbolizer 0.3.1
text: Random slopes now work: symbolize.drmTMB() reads (1 + x | group) random-effect terms mu submodel end--end. mu linear predictor renders contribution + u_{0, group()} + u_{1, group()} * x_i (index form) + Z_group u_group (matrix form). joint MVN distribution random components rendered, plus covariance-decomposition row spells 2x2 (k x k) Sigma_u terms per-component SDs within-group correlation rho. data shape extended (forward-compatibly): random_effects gains component, component_index, predictor_factor columns; variance_components gains component; new top-level slot covariance_components carries within-group correlations multi-component groups. intercept-case ((1 | group)) keeps historic simpler symbols empty covariance_components slot, existing code assumed old shape still works. Capability row drmTMB / gaussian / random_effects updated reflect broader scope; nested / crossed / RE--sigma remain Planned reserved. friendly capability gate now distinguishes two unsupported shapes: RE submodels mu, slope-RE without intercept (gets error message). group_means() group_slopes() gain scale argument ("response" (default) "link") return new scale column. release, functions returned emmeans output link scale non-identity-link families — Poisson “group mean” reported log count rate, Beta mean reported log-odds, Gamma mean log response, . easy misread response-scale value. default now "response": back-transformed mean (count rate Poisson, proportion Beta, response-scale mean Gamma, geometric mean lognormal, response-scale mean nbinom2, mean Gaussian Student-t). Pass scale = "link" get linear-predictor scale used coefficient table. lognormal fits drmTMB exposes mu identity link (mu represents log(Y)), emmeans’s automatic back-transform doesn’t fire. group_means() now tells emmeans implicit log transformation via stats::update(emm, tran = "log") response-scale output geometric mean delta-method CI. print.symbolizer_group_means() print.symbolizer_group_slopes() name scale footer (“Scale: response. CI method: wald.”).

what: v0.3 — non-Gaussian drmTMB families, polished methods_text
title: symbolizer 0.3.0
text: symbolize.drmTMB() reads four non-Gaussian families end--end via CSV-driven path: Gamma (stats::Gamma(link = "log")) — positive continuous, multiplicative mean reading response scale. Beta (drmTMB::beta()) — Y (0, 1) logit-link mean log-link precision; mean coefficients render odds ratios. Poisson (stats::poisson()) — counts dispersion parameter; mean coefficients render rate ratios. variance = mean constraint called assumption table methods_text paragraph. nbinom2 (drmTMB::nbinom2()) — counts overdispersion; size parameter (exp(sigma_i)) controls Poisson limit. family ships assumption rows, interpretation rows (per coefficient role every relevant scale), methods_text template — shortcuts, biology family genuinely differs. Capability registry rows flipped First slice drmTMB / Gamma / mu, sigma (note capital G — base R’s stats::Gamma() uses string), drmTMB / beta / mu, sigma, drmTMB / poisson / mu, drmTMB / nbinom2 / mu, sigma. methods_text(sym) biv_gaussian fits now reads cleanly three secondary submodels (sigma1, sigma2, rho12) intercept-. old output included awkward parenthesised (intercept ; intercept ) clause; polished version uses dedicated sigma_pair_clause rho12_clause slots pick one three readable phrasings (intercept-, mixed, predictors). Templates univariate families unaffected; biv_gaussian-specific three-clause shape genuinely unique . symbolize.drmTMB() reads Student-t fits (family = drmTMB::student()) end--end. Student-t adds nu (degrees--freedom) submodel alongside mu sigma; drmTMB parameterises nu log(nu - 2) scale (logm2 link) nu > 2 always enforced modelled variance nu / (nu - 2) * sigma^2 finite. structured symbolic object carries: Student-t distribution row index matrix forms, submodels mu (identity), sigma (log), nu (logm2), interpretation rows three submodels including biological reading nu explains heavier vs lighter tails, assumption row positivity_and_finite_variance capturing nu > 2 constraint, methods_text() template covering three submodels log(nu - 2) link explanation. Capability registry rows flipped “Planned reserved” “First slice”: drmTMB / student / mu drmTMB / student / sigma drmTMB / student / nu drm_link_for() now generalises multi-dpar link lookup. previous biv_gaussian-branch extended recognise family whose links exposed named vector (Student-t today; future families can land without changes ). symbolize.drmTMB() reads lognormal fits (family = drmTMB::lognormal()) end--end. conditional distribution row reads Y_i | mu_i, sigma_i ~ Lognormal(mu_i, sigma_i^2) <=> log(Y_i) | mu_i, sigma_i ~ Normal(mu_i, sigma_i^2), spelling equivalence reader sees views. Interpretation rows mu speak terms geometric mean response — unit change predictor multiplies geometric mean exp(beta). Architectural refactor: distribution LaTeX now CSV-driven. inst/extdata/family-distributions.csv carries conditional- distribution row (index + matrix form) every family. previous hardcoded family branches drm_build_distribution() drm_build_components() gone. Adding future univariate family (gamma, beta, Poisson, nbinom2, Tweedie, …) now CSV-operation. Structural-shape families (biv_gaussian, future GLLVM extensions, ordinal models) still need code components-list shape differs.

what: v0.2.1 — methods_text, per-fit warnings, biv_gaussian gate
title: symbolizer 0.2.1
text: New: warning_table(sym) returns tibble conditions symbolize() flagged building model object. row one warning code, severity (info / warn / error), templated message, context string. Prose templated inst/extdata/warning-templates.csv. Today system ships one active check: few_groups_wald (warn) — Wald 95% CI used random-effect group fewer ~10 levels. check suppressed user passes ci_method = "profile" symbolize(). model_card(sym) surfaces warnings table ’s non-empty; field also lives sym$warnings_registry raw access. New: methods_text(sym) returns draft Methods-section paragraph fitted model — kind paragraph biologist otherwise write hand paper. prose composed CSV template (inst/extdata/methods-templates.csv) using slots filled symbolized_model. LLM involved runtime; every phrase traces template row plus substituted slots. Returns symbolizer_methods_text S3 object three slots: text (assembled paragraph), slots (named substitutions), reminders (editorial reminders author). Templates ship drmTMB / gaussian, drmTMB / biv_gaussian, gllvmTMB / gaussian. Treat output draft; print method appends reminder effect. group_means() group_slopes() now gate biv_gaussian fits symbolizer layer friendly explanation, instead letting drmTMB’s emmeans preflight surface less explanatory error. marginal mean bivariate fit joint 2-vector prediction (mu1, mu2), scalar, emmeans abstraction apply. gate’s message points drmTMB::predict_parameters() fit--response-- univariate alternative. Documented roxygen functions.

what: v0.2 — bivariate Gaussian, structural comparison, article tidy
title: symbolizer 0.2.0
text: symbolize.drmTMB() reads bivariate Gaussian fits — biv_gaussian(y2 ~ ...) family drmTMB — structured surface used univariate fits. response becomes 2-vector (Y_{1i}, Y_{2i}), conditional distribution becomes MVN_2((mu_{1i}, mu_{2i}), Sigma_i), symbolic story now carries five submodels (mu1, mu2, sigma1, sigma2, rho12). New capability rows: drmTMB,biv_gaussian,{mu1,mu2,sigma1,sigma2,rho12} flip “Planned reserved” “First slice”. Per-submodel response handling: interpretation rows mu1 / sigma1 substitute response_1; mu2 / sigma2 substitute response_2; rho12 rows reference . formula_bridge carries one row per submodel including new mu1, mu2, sigma1, sigma2, rho12 parts; rho12 meaning reads “Fisher-z residual correlation {response_1} {response_2} linear function correlation-model predictors”. Interpretation templates assumption templates gain biv_gaussian rows (inst/extdata/interpretation-templates.csv inst/extdata/assumption-templates.csv). New: compare_symbolic(sym_a, sym_b, metrics = FALSE) returns structural diff two symbolized_model objects. Slots: meta (left / right model summaries — class, family, response, n_obs), diff_submodels (presence per submodel: left_only / right_only / ), diff_terms (presence per (submodel, term_label) pair), diff_assumptions (status side plus same_status flag). S3 class symbolic_comparison; print() produces structured cli block knit_print() produces side--side markdown tables. Passing metrics = TRUE adds fifth slot diff_metrics AIC, BIC, log-likelihood, df side plus delta (right - left); metrics block refuses compute deltas two fits obviously incomparable (different family, response, n_obs) instead carries comparable = FALSE attribute plus note explaining . fit-time identifiability convergence diagnostics, run drmTMB::check_drm() (gllvmTMB analogue) per fit interpreting structural diff.
